knowledge_point.title: Using the Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Expressions

question.:question/problem:
Express

$$
12\cos^{4}\left(5^\circ\right)-12\sin^{4}\left(5^\circ\right)
$$

as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the difference of squares, then the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&12\cos^{4}\left(5^\circ\right)-12\sin^{4}\left(5^\circ\right) \\
&=12\left(\cos^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)-\sin^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)\right) \\
&\qquad\cdot\left(\cos^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)+\sin^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\cos^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)+\sin^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)=1$, this reduces to

$$
12\left(\cos^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)-\sin^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)\right).
$$

Recall the **double-angle formula for cosine**:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).
$$

Substitute $x=5^\circ$ and double the angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&12\left(\cos^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)-\sin^{2}\left(5^\circ\right)\right) \\
&=12\cos\left(2\cdot 5^\circ\right) \\
&=12\cos\left(10^\circ\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Only the angle doubles; the common coefficient stays outside the cosine.
